title: Human Impact and Sustainability
seo_title: Grade 7 Science: Human Impact and Sustainability Worksheets (Ontario Curriculum)
standard_text: Assess the effects of human activities on ecosystems, including pollution, bioaccumulation and habitat loss; evaluate sustainable practices, including Indigenous perspectives such as Seven Generations thinking. (summary of the Ontario Science and Technology curriculum, 2022, Strand B: Life Systems – Interactions in the Environment)
meta_desc: Free Grade 7 science worksheets on human impact on ecosystems, pollution, bioaccumulation, the 3 Rs and sustainable choices. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Pollution and habitat loss harm ecosystems; sustainable choices protect them for the future.
body_html:
How to think about it

People change ecosystems by building, farming, polluting and using resources.

  • Toxins such as mercury and pesticides build up in food chains (bioaccumulation and biomagnification).
  • Sustainability means meeting our needs without harming future generations.
  • Reduce, reuse, recycle, protect habitats and restore damaged areas.
Example

Why do eagles have more pesticide than fish?

toxins build up at each level

Answer: biomagnification

Example

Which of the 3 Rs is best?

not making waste at all

Answer: reduce

Common mistakes

  • Thinking recycling alone solves waste problems.
  • Thinking toxins spread out evenly in a food chain.
  • Thinking one person's choices do not matter.

faq.a: The build-up of a toxic substance in an organism's body over time.
A way of using resources that can continue for a long time without harming the environment, like replanting forests.

faq.q: What does Seven Generations thinking mean?
faq.a: Making decisions that will still be good for people seven generations into the future.

items.q: Ethan observes: “Cars and factories burn fossil fuels.” What impact can this have?
c: algae blooms that use up oxygen and kill fish
animals swallowing or getting tangled in plastic
air pollution and more carbon dioxide
items.e: Human activities can change Earth's systems.

items.q: Priya's class studies this problem: “Forests are cleared for new houses.” Which solution would best reduce the impact?
c: public transit, electric vehicles and cleaner power
keeping protected green spaces and wildlife corridors
rain gardens and permeable sidewalk that soak up runoff
planting grass buffer strips along the river and using less fertilizer
items.e: A good solution targets the cause of the impact.

items.q: Noah wants to know whether fewer fish die after a farm uses less fertilizer. What is the best way to monitor this?
c: count fish and measure oxygen in the river over several years
ask one neighbour what they think
check once on a single day
items.e: Monitoring uses measurements over time, before and after.

items.q: Microplastics are found in the Great Lakes. Where do many of them come from?
c: broken-down plastic waste and fibres from washing synthetic clothes
items.e: Microplastics are eaten by small animals.

items.q: Nathan wants to know whether a wildlife bridge reduces animal deaths. What is the best way to monitor this?
c: check once on a single day
count animals hit on the road before and after the bridge
ask one neighbour what they think
items.e: Monitoring uses measurements over time, before and after.

items.q: Which of these causes noise pollution?
c: old furniture dumped at the back of a block of flats
chemicals from a factory poured into a river
smoke from a ship's engine at sea
items.e: Construction work all night leads to noise pollution.

items.q: Which of these causes land pollution?
c: smoke from a ship's engine at sea
loud music played near a nature reserve
old furniture dumped at the back of a block of flats
paint washed into a monsoon drain
items.e: Old furniture dumped at the back of a block of flats leads to land pollution.

items.q: Benjamin wants to know whether a recycling program reduces garbage. What is the best way to monitor this?
c: weigh the garbage sent to the landfill each week before and after
check once on a single day
ask one neighbour what they think
items.e: Monitoring uses measurements over time, before and after.

items.q: Benjamin observes: “Fertilizer runs off farms into a river.” What impact can this have?
c: algae blooms that use up oxygen and kill fish
animals swallowing or getting tangled in plastic
warmer water with less oxygen for fish
items.e: Human activities can change Earth's systems.

items.q: Kai observes: “Forests are cleared for new houses.” What impact can this have?
c: warmer water with less oxygen for fish
air pollution and more carbon dioxide
animals swallowing or getting tangled in plastic
items.e: Human activities can change Earth's systems.

items.q: What is a green roof?
c: a roof covered with plants that provides habitat and absorbs rainwater
a roof made of grass clippings only
items.e: Toronto requires green roofs on some new buildings.

items.q: How do protected areas like Algonquin Park help sustainability?
c: They keep ecosystems intact for wildlife and future generations.
items.e: Protected areas preserve biodiversity.

items.q: Which is a sustainable forestry practice?
c: clear-cutting a whole valley and leaving it bare
planting new trees after cutting and leaving buffer zones near streams
items.e: Ontario requires forests to be renewed.

items.q: Aiden's class studies this problem: “Cars and factories burn fossil fuels.” Which solution would best reduce the impact?
c: rain gardens and permeable sidewalk that soak up runoff
reusable bags and bans on single-use plastic
public transit, electric vehicles and cleaner power
keeping protected green spaces and wildlife corridors
items.e: A good solution targets the cause of the impact.

items.q: Which of these causes land pollution?
c: exhaust fumes from cars and buses
old batteries thrown into the soil
items.e: Old batteries thrown into the soil leads to land pollution.

items.q: Maya observes: “Plastic bags blow into the ocean.” What impact can this have?
c: algae blooms that use up oxygen and kill fish
air pollution and more carbon dioxide
animals swallowing or getting tangled in plastic
items.e: Human activities can change Earth's systems.

items.q: Which of these causes air pollution?
c: chemicals from a factory poured into a river
exhaust fumes from cars and buses
items.e: Exhaust fumes from cars and buses leads to air pollution.

items.q: Which of these causes land pollution?
c: loud music played near a nature reserve
items.e: Garbage dumped in a forest leads to land pollution.

items.q: Which of these causes air pollution?
c: fireworks set off near a bird sanctuary
old batteries thrown into the soil
chemicals from a factory poured into a river
items.e: Smoke from factory chimneys leads to air pollution.

items.q: How did the reintroduction of elk to parts of Ontario affect ecosystems?
c: It restored a native grazing species and its role in the ecosystem.
It had no effect at all.
items.e: Restoring species can rebuild ecosystems.

items.q: Which kind of pollution is caused by aircraft taking off near homes?
items.e: Loud sounds disturb people and animals.

items.q: Why do top predators like loons and eagles have the most pesticide in their bodies?
c: The toxin becomes more concentrated at each step of the food chain (biomagnification).
items.e: DDT once harmed bald eagles in Ontario.

items.q: Why are insect pollinators such as bees important to farmers?
c: Many crops need insects to carry pollen so that fruits and seeds form.
items.e: Plants and animals depend on each other.

items.q: What is interdependence?
c: Living things in an ecosystem depend on each other for food, shelter and pollination.
items.e: Plants and animals depend on each other.

items.q: Which kind of pollution is caused by old batteries thrown into the soil?
items.e: The pollutant goes into the land.

The food chain is grass → insect → shrew → owl. How many times greater is the concentration in the shrew than in the insect?
Why are wetlands called 'the kidneys of the landscape'?
items.e: Wetlands also reduce flooding.

items.q: Which kind of pollution is caused by honking horns in heavy traffic?
items.e: Loud sounds disturb people and animals.

items.q: What does the Indigenous idea of 'Seven Generations' teach?
c: to think about how our decisions will affect people seven generations from now
items.e: It is a long-term view of sustainability.

items.q: What could happen to apple harvests if bee numbers fall a lot?
c: Fewer flowers are pollinated, so fewer apples grow.
items.e: Plants and animals depend on each other.

items.q:
OrganismConcentration of a pesticide (ppm)
seaweed0.04
periwinkle0.4
crab4.0
gull40.0
The food chain is seaweed → periwinkle → crab → gull. Why does the concentration increase along the chain?
c: The poison is diluted at each step.
The poison is made by the animals.
Each animal eats many of the one below, and the poison is not broken down or excreted.
items.e: Bioaccumulation.

The food chain is plankton → small fish → seal → polar bear. How many times greater is the concentration in the seal than in the small fish?

The food chain is oak leaves → caterpillar → blue tit → sparrowhawk. Which organism has the lowest concentration?
items.e: The producer at the bottom.

algae0.04

The food chain is algae → water flea → minnow → pike. How many times greater is the concentration in the minnow than in the water flea?
Which kind of pollution is caused by construction work all night?
items.e: Loud sounds disturb people and animals.

items.q: Which kind of pollution is caused by old furniture dumped at the back of a block of flats?
items.e: The pollutant goes into the land.

items.q:
OrganismConcentration of a pesticide (ppm)
algae0.02
water flea0.2
minnow2.0
pike20.0
The food chain is algae → water flea → minnow → pike. Which organism has the highest concentration of the poison?
items.e: The top predator: poison builds up at each level.

items.q: Which kind of pollution is caused by smoke from factory chimneys?
items.e: The pollutant goes into the air.

items.q: What is sustainability?
c: meeting our needs without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs
using resources as fast as possible
items.e: Sustainable choices protect ecosystems.

items.q: Which kind of pollution is caused by detergent washed into a drain?
items.e: The pollutant goes into the water.

items.q: Which of the 3Rs is shown by putting drink cans into the blue recycling bin?
items.e: Recycle means the material is made into something new.

items.q: Which of the 3Rs is shown by using old newspapers to wrap fragile things?
items.e: Reuse means using something again without changing what it is made of.

items.q: Which of the 3Rs is shown by buying drinks in large bottles instead of many small ones?
items.e: Reduce means using less in the first place.

items.q: Students pick up litter at East Coast Park. What is the most likely effect on the environment?
c: It has no effect on living things.
items.e: Protecting habitats helps living things; destroying or polluting them causes harm.

items.q: Zoe's family throws away 30 kg of garbage in 10 days. If they recycle 40% of it instead, how much less garbage goes to be burnt?
items.e: 40% of 30 kg = 12 kg.

items.q: Olivia observes: “Rainwater carries oil and garbage from parking lots into streams.” What impact can this have?
c: warmer water with less oxygen for fish
animals swallowing or getting tangled in plastic
air pollution and more carbon dioxide
items.e: Human activities can change Earth's systems.

items.q: Mateo's family throws away 3.5 kg of garbage a day. How much garbage is this in one week?
items.e: 3.5 kg × 7 days = 24.5 kg.

items.q: Why are road salt levels a concern for Ontario streams?
c: Salt washes into streams in spring and can harm fish and plants.
items.e: Using less salt protects streams.

items.q: Green roofs with plants are built on top of buildings. What is the most likely effect on the environment?
c: It has no effect on living things.
items.e: Protecting habitats helps living things; destroying or polluting them causes harm.

items.q: People release unwanted pet terrapins into a reservoir. What is the most likely effect on the environment?
c: It has no effect on living things.
items.e: This destroys or disturbs a habitat, so living things are harmed.

items.q: A nature reserve is set up to protect a forest. What is the most likely effect on the environment?
c: It has no effect on living things.
items.e: Protecting habitats helps living things; destroying or polluting them causes harm.

items.q: Arjun's family throws away 25 kg of garbage in 10 days. If they recycle 25% of it instead, how much less garbage goes to be burnt?
How does urban sprawl affect ecosystems?
c: It replaces natural habitats with roads and buildings.
items.e: Green spaces help reduce the impact.

items.q: Which action reduces your ecological footprint?
c: walking, cycling or taking transit instead of driving
items.e: Less energy and waste means a smaller footprint.

items.q: Which of the 3Rs is shown by taking old phones to an e-waste bin?
items.e: Recycle means the material is made into something new.

items.q: Which of the 3Rs is shown by giving old clothes to a younger cousin?
items.e: Reuse means using something again without changing what it is made of.

items.q: Fishermen use nets that also catch turtles. What is the most likely effect on the environment?
c: It has no effect on living things.
items.e: This destroys or disturbs a habitat, so living things are harmed.

items.q: Ethan's family throws away 2.5 kg of garbage a day. How much garbage is this in one week?
items.e: 2.5 kg × 7 days = 17.5 kg.

items.q: Arjun's family throws away 2 kg of garbage a day. How much garbage is this in one week?
items.e: 2 kg × 7 days = 14 kg.

items.q: Which of the 3Rs is shown by putting used paper cartons into the recycling bin?
items.e: Recycle means the material is made into something new.

items.q: What does 'reduce' mean in the 3Rs?
c: making something new from old material
items.e: Reduce is the best of the 3Rs.

items.q: How can a growing population affect habitats?
c: More land is used for homes, farms and roads.
items.e: Land use increases.

items.q: How does cutting down forests affect animals?
c: They lose their food and shelter.
items.e: Clearing forests destroys habitats.

items.q: Which two things together determine a population's total use of resources?
c: the number of people and how much each person uses
only the size of the country
items.e: Total = people × use per person.

items.q: Can individual choices matter for the environment?
c: Yes. Many people making small changes adds up.
items.e: Per-capita use times many people.

items.q: What is bioaccumulation?
c: the build-up of a toxic substance in an organism over time
items.e: Mercury can build up in fish.

items.q: Why is monitoring important after a solution is put in place?
c: to make the solution more expensive
to check with data whether it actually reduces the impact
items.e: Data shows if it works.

items.q: Why should plastic bags not be thrown into the sea?
c: Turtles may swallow them and die.
items.e: Plastic takes hundreds of years to break down.

items.q: What is composting?
c: letting decomposers break food and yard waste into rich soil
items.e: Composting keeps waste out of landfills.

items.q: Which gas is mainly linked to global warming?
items.e: Burning fuels releases carbon dioxide.

items.q: Oil spilled from a ship coats the feathers of seabirds. What happens to the birds?
c: They cannot fly or keep warm, and may die.
items.e: Oil spills are water pollution.

items.q: Why are nature reserves such as Sungei Buloh important?
c: They are places to dump garbage.
They are only for building houses.
They protect habitats so plants and animals can survive.
items.e: Conservation keeps many populations alive.

items.q: Why does cutting down many trees increase the amount of carbon dioxide in the air?
c: Trees give out carbon dioxide only.
Carbon dioxide comes from the soil.
Fewer trees take in carbon dioxide for photosynthesis.
items.e: Burning the trees also releases carbon dioxide.

items.q: What is per-capita consumption?
c: the amount of a resource used per person
items.e: Per capita means per person.

items.q: How can fertilizer runoff harm a lake?
c: It causes algae to grow quickly, and when the algae die, oxygen levels drop.
items.e: This is called eutrophication.

items.q: Which change helps reduce air pollution?
c: using renewable energy instead of burning coal
items.e: Less burning, cleaner air.

items.q: Which of these is caused by people?
c: a river flooding after heavy rain
leaves rotting on the forest floor
clearing a forest to build houses
a tree falling in a storm
items.e: People change the environment in many ways.

items.q: What is runoff pollution?
c: pollution carried by rainwater from land into streams and lakes
items.e: Fertilizer and oil wash into water.

items.q: Which action helps to save electricity?
c: keeping lights on in empty rooms
leaving the TV on standby all night
setting the air-conditioner to 25 °C and closing the windows
items.e: Making electricity usually means burning fuel.

items.q: Which is a benefit of buying local food?
c: less fuel is used to transport it
items.e: Shorter trips mean fewer emissions.

items.q: A canal had many fish. After a factory poured waste into it, many fish died. Which is the most likely reason?
c: The waste polluted the water and reduced the oxygen in it.
items.e: Pollution harms the organisms in the habitat.

items.q: Kai's town has 1000 people. Each person makes about 4 kg of plastic per person each month. About how much does the town make in all?
Noah learns: Sea otters were overhunted. What happened to the sea urchins?
c: They increased and ate the kelp forests.
items.e: A change to one part of an ecosystem affects other populations.

items.q: By how much did native plants decrease from 2015 to 2019 in Maya's data?
Why does planting trees in a city help to cool it?
c: Trees give shade and lose water vapour from their leaves.
items.e: Green spaces are cooler than bare concrete.

items.q: Emma's town has 20 000 people who each use 5 kg of garbage per person each day. If the population doubles and each person uses the same amount, what is the new total?
items.e: Twice the people × the same use = twice the total.

items.q: By how much did frogs decrease from 2015 to 2019 in Chloe's data?
Ethan's town has 2000 people who each use 4 kg of garbage per person each day. If the population doubles and each person uses the same amount, what is the new total?
items.e: Twice the people × the same use = twice the total.

items.q: A town's population stays the same, but each person buys twice as much plastic. What happens to the town's plastic waste?
items.e: Per-capita use matters as much as population.

items.q: Ethan argues that a city of 1 million people using 100 litres of water each per day uses more water than a city of 2 million using 40 litres each. Is he right?
c: Yes: 100 million litres vs. 80 million litres.
No, the bigger city always uses more.
items.e: Multiply people by use per person.

items.q: Ethan learns: Zebra mussels spread in a lake. What happened to the native mussels?
c: They decreased because zebra mussels outcompeted them for food.
items.e: A change to one part of an ecosystem affects other populations.

items.q: Arjun's town has 1000 people who each use 2 litres of gasoline per person each week. If everyone cuts use in half, what is the new total?
items.e: Halving use per person halves the total, even with the same population.

items.q: Zoe's town has 5000 people who each use 5 litres of gasoline per person each week. If everyone cuts use in half, what is the new total?
items.e: Halving use per person halves the total, even with the same population.

items.q: By how much did songbirds decrease from 2015 to 2019 in Liam's data?
By how much did songbirds decrease from 2015 to 2019 in Emma's data?
Ava learns: A drought dried a pond. What happened to the frogs?
c: They decreased because they lost water and food.
They moved into the trees permanently.
items.e: A change to one part of an ecosystem affects other populations.

items.q: By how much did frogs decrease from 2015 to 2019 in Noah's data?
Ava's school puts in recycling bins. Landfill garbage drops from 400 kg to 250 kg a week. How much less garbage is that?
Why should scientists collect data for several years when monitoring a river?
c: Natural changes from year to year could hide or exaggerate the effect.
items.e: Long-term data is stronger evidence.

items.q: A school collected 40 kg of paper for recycling each month. How does this help the environment?
c: More garbage goes to the landfill.
Fewer trees need to be cut down to make new paper.
items.e: Recycling saves raw materials.
